_note:
Plain-English glosses for the abbreviation signs that actually occur in the exercise bank. `status` is load-bearing: `verified` = the expansion comes from a source AND the source page was read as an image (the chocomufin table shipped with the Eutyches dataset; Thompson 1912; Cappelli 1929 -- see research/cappelli-index.md for the leaf of every sign); `proposed` = standard palaeographic convention, mine, AWAITING WILSON'S RATIFICATION. Never silently promote one to the other. `mechanism` follows Thompson 1912 ch. VII: a CONTRACTION keeps the word's ending so the inflection survives; a SUSPENSION cuts the end off and destroys it.

⭐ SCOPE, added 2026-08-28 with the Syriac track. A gloss keyed to a CHARACTER is self-scoping — a Tironian et cannot occur in Syriac. A gloss keyed to a TRIGGER regex is not: the word-division gloss matches ‘three short words in a row’, which is true of every script on earth, and it fired on 37 of 110 Syriac lines with a note about `quarequomodolongitudinem`. Every trigger gloss now names the `profiles` it belongs to. Absent `profiles` still means ‘everywhere’, which is right for a character.

signs.name: the abbreviation stroke
signs.short: a stroke over a letter: something has been left out
signs.note: The commonest mark in Latin manuscripts, and the least specific — it says only that letters are missing. Over a vowel it is an omitted m or n (Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV: cōdo=conditio, ī=in). Over a c it is cum, con, cen (p. XXX) — in this book c̃sidero is considero. At a word's end it can be -er: frequent̃ is frequenter. Cappelli devotes a whole section to signs like this — segni abbreviativi con significato relativo, p. XXIX — signs whose value is not fixed but changes with the letter they are attached to. That is why an abbreviation table can never be a simple list of one sign, one meaning.

signs.name: u with a stroke
signs.short: ũ = un or um
signs.note: A vowel carrying the stroke has lost a following m or n. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV lists the mark first of all — I. — = m, n — and notes that with the value of m it was used constantly in the Middle Ages for the endings am, em, um. His own examples include actū = actum. This is the commonest abbreviation in the corpus; learn it before anything else.

signs.name: a with a stroke
signs.short: ã = an or am
signs.note: A vowel carrying the stroke has lost a following m or n. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV lists the mark first of all — I. — = m, n — and notes that with the value of m it was used constantly in the Middle Ages for the endings am, em, um. His own examples include aliā = aliam. This is the commonest abbreviation in the corpus; learn it before anything else.

signs.name: o with a stroke
signs.short: õ = on or om
signs.note: A vowel carrying the stroke has lost a following m or n. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV lists the mark first of all — I. — = m, n — and notes that with the value of m it was used constantly in the Middle Ages for the endings am, em, um. His own examples include cōmūe = commune — note the doubled m is not written twice. This is the commonest abbreviation in the corpus; learn it before anything else.

signs.name: i with a stroke
signs.short: ĩ = in or im
signs.note: A vowel carrying the stroke has lost a following m or n. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV lists the mark first of all — I. — = m, n — and notes that with the value of m it was used constantly in the Middle Ages for the endings am, em, um. His own examples include ī = in, often the whole word. This is the commonest abbreviation in the corpus; learn it before anything else.

signs.name: p with a stroke through the descender
signs.short: ꝑ = per (also par, por)
signs.note: The stroke crosses the descender of the p. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXX, gives it as per, par… por… — read confirmed on the plate. Its near neighbour ꝓ, with a loop rather than a bar, is pro (Cappelli p. XXXVIII); learn the two as a pair so you never confuse them.

signs.name: q with a stroke through the descender
signs.short: ꝗ = qui — but see the date
signs.note: Cappelli p. XXX gives q̶ = qui. ⚠ His footnote matters for us: “Nel sec. VIII lo stesso segno vale que” — in the eighth century the same sign means que, and in Anglo-Saxon writing quam or quia. Our manuscripts are ninth-century, sitting right on that boundary, so read the sentence before you trust the sign.

signs.name: a written above the line
signs.short: a small a above a letter supplies that vowel — qͣ = qua
signs.note: A vowel written small and high belongs immediately after the letter it sits on. Over a q it gives qua: aliqͣ is aliqua, qͣsi is quasi. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV groups these under IV. = r, re, ra, ar, a — the same family of superscript strokes also supplies an r, so read what follows before deciding. Once you see it as a letter that has simply climbed above the line it stops being strange.

signs.name: the us-sign
signs.short: ꝰ = -us
signs.note: A word-ending sign, standing on the line after the last written letter: c̃seruatꝰ is conservatus. Verified against the character table shipped with this dataset.

signs.name: the ur-sign
signs.short: ᷑ = -ur
signs.note: A small hook above the line at a word's end: seruat᷑ is seruatur. This one matters for reading sense, because -ur is what makes a Latin verb passive. Verified against this dataset's character table.

signs.name: the est-sign
signs.short: ÷ = est
signs.note: A whole word in one mark. Its dataset character table names it outright, and Thompson gives the same. When a sentence seems to have no verb, look for this.

signs.name: the Tironian et
signs.short: ⁊ = et
signs.note: Not a letter at all: a surviving sign from the ancient Roman shorthand attributed to Cicero's secretary Tiro. It outlived the rest of that system by a thousand years, and is still written in Irish today.

signs.name: l with a stroke
signs.short: ł = vel (and, inside a word, ul or el)
signs.note: Cappelli p. XXX: ł = vel, ul…, …el. So it is not always the word ‘or’: crossing the ascender of an l mid-word it can simply supply ul or el. In a grammar book, which spends its life saying a form may be this or that, vel is still much the likeliest.

signs.name: d with a stroke
signs.short: đ = a d-word, most often quod as qđ
signs.note: Rarely alone. You will nearly always meet it as qđ = quod.

signs.name: e caudata, the e with a tail
signs.short: ę = ae
signs.note: Not an abbreviation at all but a spelling: the little tail is how the Middle Ages wrote the diphthong ae. ecclesię is ecclesiae. If you read it as a plain e, the case ending will mislead you. ⚠ Deliberately not verified against Cappelli: his Lexicon catalogues abbreviation signs, and this is not one — it is a way of spelling ae. Its absence there is a confirmation, not a gap.

signs.name: round brackets — the editors' supply
signs.short: ( ) = letters supplied because the ink cannot be read
signs.note: These letters are not on the page. Where the ink is lost the editors restored what the word must have been and put it in brackets. Verified by reading the manuscript itself at four places: purple mould stains sitting over the words; ink simply worn away; a gloss too faint to make out; and, in one case, a tear that has taken the parchment clean away. Do not hunt for them in the ink — there is nothing there. Damage of this kind is ordinary; a thousand-year-old book has been rained on, handled, and eaten by mould, and part of reading manuscripts is knowing what your edition is quietly doing for you.

signs.name: the enlarged opening initial
signs.short: a big letter out in the margin — it is the word's first letter
signs.note: A new section opens with a large decorated capital set out in the margin, clear of the ruled text block and often two lines deep. The scribe does not write the letter twice. So the ordinary script begins with the SECOND letter: the line here starts uaeritur, the tall Q beside it supplies the first, and together they are Quaeritur. Verified on the page (Cod. 940 f. 30). Once you know to look for it this is a help rather than a trap — it tells you a new argument is beginning.

signs.name: the et-ligature
signs.short: & is e and t written as one — and it works INSIDE a word
signs.note: Our ampersand began life as a ligature of e and t, and in a manuscript it has not yet settled into meaning only the word et. The scribe uses it for the letters e-t wherever they fall, including in the middle or at the end of a word: this line's ink reads ſupl& and the word is suplet. Likewise hab& for habet, man& for manet. ⚠ Do not confuse it with the Tironian ⁊, which is a shorthand sign for the word et and never supplies a syllable. Verified on the page (Cod. 940 f. 41).

signs.name: word division
signs.short: the gaps between words are not where you expect them
signs.note: Ancient books were written in scriptio continua — no spaces at all. Word division was introduced gradually, and in the ninth century the job is only half done. Short words cling to their neighbours, and a gap can open in the middle of a long one. On this page the ink reads quarequomodolongitudinem where the print gives Quare quomodo longitudinem. ⚑ So do not trust the gaps. Read a run of letters, find a word you know inside it, and let the rest fall out — the Latin divides the line, not the spacing. This is the single thing that most often defeats a reader who can already name every letter.

signs.name: the line-break mark
signs.short: the word is not finished — it continues on the next line
signs.note: A scribe fits the line to the ruling, not to the words, so a word breaks wherever the margin arrives and carries on below. The transcription marks the break ¬; in the ink it is a small stroke at the very end of the line, and sometimes nothing at all. Read on this page: the line ends …arboris ge¬ and the next begins nerę — together generę. ⚑ The break falls wherever it falls, with no regard for syllables you would recognise, so never try to make sense of the fragment on its own. Several lines in this bank are cut from the middle of a sentence for the same reason.

signs.name: kappa, in two strokes
signs.short: κ is made of two separate marks that often do not touch
signs.note: In print the arms of a kappa spring from its upright. This scribe writes it in two pen-strokes — an upright, and a small detached arc for the arms — and the two commonly do not meet. Magnified on this manuscript the gap is plain. Until you expect it, a κ reads as two unrelated marks, or as a stray stroke beside a letter you cannot name. Verified on the page (Pal. gr. 23, f. 174).

signs.name: ligatures
signs.short: pairs of letters fused into one shape
signs.note: This is the difficulty the Greek track exists for. Writing at speed, the scribe runs letters together into a single compound shape that may resemble neither of its parts — ει, ου, στ, σθ are the commonest. ⚑ Do not try to find the letters inside the shape. Learn the shape whole, as its own sign, the way you learned &. That is why this track asks you to look before it asks you to type.

signs.name: rho with alpha
signs.short: the alpha rides high on the rho, not beside it
signs.note: Where rho is followed by alpha, the alpha is often written small and high, tucked against the rho's shoulder rather than set beside it on the line. The pair reads as one mark with a tail. ⚠ Proposed, not yet verified — this manuscript's images are not sharp enough at letter scale for me to confirm it, so treat it as a hint to test with your own eye rather than a settled fact.

signs.name: omega like a figure eight
signs.short: ω can look like an 8 lying on its side
signs.note: The printed omega is a cup with two humps. In this hand the pen frequently closes both curves, giving a shape much closer to a figure eight on its side — and in the common ending -ῶν it carries a circumflex on top, which closes it further. ⚠ Proposed, not yet verified at letter scale on this witness.

signs.name: seyame, the two dots of the plural
signs.short: two dots over a word: it is plural
signs.note: Two dots set over a letter of the word — seyame — mark it as a plural. They are not tied to a fixed letter: in this manuscript they sit over a ܪ 455 times, a ܝ 286 times, and so on down. ܟܗ̈ܢܐ is kāhnē, priests; without the dots the same four letters are a singular. They fall on 1,182 of the 2,475 lines of this witness, so you will meet them at once. ⚑ Miss them and you have not made a small error — you have read a different word.

signs.name: the dot above
signs.short: a single dot ABOVE: which of two words this is
signs.note: With no vowels written, a single dot does the work. Above a verb it marks the participle: ܐܡ̇ܪ āmar, ‘he says’, 167 times here — against ܐܡ̣ܪ with the dot below, emar, ‘he said’, 79 times. Above a ܡܢ it gives man, ‘who’. Over a final ܗ it makes the suffix feminine: ܠܗ̇ ‘to her’ (40×) against ܠܗ ‘to him’ (232×).

signs.name: the dot below
signs.short: a single dot BELOW: the other of the two
signs.note: The counterpart of the dot above, and the pair is the lesson of this track. Below a verb it marks the perfect: ܐܡ̣ܪ emar, ‘he said’. Below ܡܢ it gives men, ‘from’ (179×), where the dot above gives man, ‘who’ (49×) — and 217 times this scribe writes it bare and lets the sentence decide. ⚑ In this bank 675 word-forms out of 7,035 exist in more than one pointing. The dots are not ornament.

signs.name: the abbreviation mark
signs.short: a suspended word, cut short
signs.note: Syriac's one abbreviation sign, and after the Latin tracks it is a holiday: it occurs on 140 lines out of 2,475 and there is essentially nothing else. It marks a word written short, most often ܬܠܡܝ̈ܕ܏ܘܗܝ for talmīdaw(hy), ‘his disciples’. A 16th-century Gospel book copied for a patron is written out, not squeezed.
